content: The antiviral drug ritonavir increases the levels or effects of norethindrone by inhibiting the hepatic and intestinal enzyme CYP3A4, which is responsible for its metabolism. Similarly, ritonavir increases the levels or effects of norgestrel through the same mechanism. Caution and monitoring are advised when these drugs are co-administered. Ritonavir also increases the levels or effects of oliceridine by affecting CYP3A4 metabolism. If co-administration is necessary, less frequent oliceridine dosing may be required. Close monitoring for respiratory depression and sedation is essential, and subsequent doses should be titrated accordingly. If ritonavir is discontinued, oliceridine dosage may need to be increased to maintain stable drug effects, with monitoring for signs of opioid withdrawal. Ritonavir increases the levels or effects of nortriptyline by inhibiting the hepatic enzyme CYP2D6. Caution and monitoring are recommended. Conversely, ritonavir decreases the levels of olanzapine by increasing its metabolism, necessitating caution and monitoring. Ritonavir also increases the levels or effects of oliceridine by inhibiting CYP2D6 metabolism. Similar precautions as with CYP3A4 inhibition apply, including less frequent dosing, close monitoring for respiratory depression and sedation, and dose adjustments if ritonavir is discontinued. Both ritonavir and inhaled olodaterol prolong the QTc interval, increasing the risk of ventricular arrhythmias. Caution and monitoring are advised, especially in patients with cardiovascular risk factors. Similarly, lopinavir and olodaterol also prolong the QTc interval, requiring the same precautions. Ritonavir increases the levels or effects of omeprazole by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Caution and monitoring are recommended. Lopinavir and ondansetron both prolong the QTc interval, and their combination should be avoided in patients with congenital long QT syndrome. ECG monitoring is recommended when co-administered with other QT-prolonging medications, electrolyte abnormalities, congestive heart failure (CHF), or bradyarrhythmias. Ritonavir increases the levels or effects of ondansetron by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Caution and monitoring are advised. Orlistat decreases the levels or effects of ritonavir by inhibiting gastrointestinal absorption, which applies only to the oral forms of both agents. Loss of virological control has been reported in HIV-infected patients taking orlistat with antiretroviral drugs, possibly due to reduced systemic absorption. Frequent monitoring of HIV RNA levels is recommended, and orlistat should be discontinued if an increased viral load is confirmed. Ritonavir increases the levels or effects of osilodrostat by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Therapy modification and close monitoring are necessary. Lopinavir has a similar effect on osilodrostat, requiring the same precautions. Both osilodrostat and lopinavir prolong the QTc interval, necessitating caution and monitoring. Osimertinib and lopinavir both prolong the QTc interval, requiring periodic ECG and electrolyte monitoring in patients taking QT-prolonging drugs. Ritonavir increases the levels of ospemifene by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism, and caution is advised. Lopinavir also increases ospemifene levels through the same mechanism but decreases them by affecting CYP2C19 metabolism. Monitoring is recommended. Oxaliplatin increases lopinavir levels or effects through other mechanisms, necessitating ECG monitoring in patients at risk of QT prolongation. Oxcarbazepine decreases lopinavir and ritonavir levels by inducing CYP3A4 metabolism, requiring caution and monitoring. Ritonavir increases oxymorphone levels by inhibiting CYP2D6 metabolism. Caution and monitoring are advised. Both ozanimod and lopinavir prolong the QTc interval, and ozanimod treatment should generally not be initiated in patients concurrently taking QT-prolonging drugs with known arrhythmogenic properties. Ritonavir increases ozanimod levels through other mechanisms, requiring therapy modification and close monitoring. Ritonavir increases paclitaxel levels by inhibiting the P-glycoprotein (MDR1) efflux transporter and other mechanisms. Therapy modification and close monitoring are necessary, as paclitaxel toxicity may increase when co-administered with CYP2C8 inhibitors. Ritonavir also increases the levels of protein-bound paclitaxel through similar mechanisms, requiring the same precautions. Ritonavir increases paliperidone levels by inhibiting the P-glycoprotein efflux transporter. Caution and monitoring are recommended. Lopinavir increases panobinostat levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism, necessitating therapy modification and close monitoring. Ritonavir has a similar effect on panobinostat, and the starting dose of panobinostat should be reduced to 10 mg when co-administered with strong CYP3A4 inhibitors. Lopinavir increases paricalcitol levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism, and caution is advised. Ritonavir has a similar effect on paricalcitol, increasing the potential for toxicity. Ritonavir also increases paromomycin levels by inhibiting the P-glycoprotein efflux transporter, requiring caution and monitoring. Lopinavir and pasireotide both prolong the QTc interval, necessitating therapy modification and close monitoring. Ritonavir increases paroxetine levels by inhibiting CYP2D6 metabolism, requiring caution and monitoring. Peginterferon alfa-2b may alter the therapeutic effects of CYP2D6 substrates, and caution is advised when co-administered with antiretroviral protease inhibitors due to the potential for hepatic damage. Pentobarbital decreases lopinavir and ritonavir levels by inducing CYP3A4 metabolism, requiring caution and monitoring. Ritonavir increases perampanel levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism, necessitating caution and monitoring. Phenobarbital decreases lopinavir and ritonavir levels by inducing CYP3A4 metabolism and inhibiting the P-glycoprotein efflux transporter. Caution and monitoring are recommended. Phenytoin decreases ritonavir and lopinavir levels through similar mechanisms, requiring the same precautions. Ritonavir increases pitavastatin toxicity through other mechanisms, such as OATP1B1 inhibition, which may increase the risk of myopathy. Caution and monitoring are advised. Lopinavir increases polatuzumab vedotin levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism, and caution is recommended. Polatuzumab undergoes catabolism to small peptides, amino acids, and monomethyl auristatin E (MMAE), a CYP3A4 substrate. Ritonavir increases pitolisant levels by inhibiting CYP2D6 metabolism. Therapy modification and close monitoring are necessary, with the pitolisant dose reduced by half when initiating strong CYP2D6 inhibitors.
